title: High-Risk Windows Token Privileges Enabled
exclusions: This use case reports Windows Security Event ID 4703 when `EnabledPrivilegeList` shows one or more explicitly selected high-risk privileges: `SeCreateTokenPrivilege`, `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege`, `SeImpersonatePrivilege`, `SeTcbPrivilege`, `SeDebugPrivilege`, or `SeLoadDriverPrivilege`. Event 4703 records privileges enabled or disabled in an existing account token; this rule evaluates only the enabled list. It does not prove access-token theft, impersonation, primary-token assignment, process creation with a token, credential dumping, code injection, or driver loading, and it does not cover privilege assignment/removal in local policy (4704/4705), sensitive privilege use (4673/4674), special privileges assigned at logon (4672), Sysmon process access (10), or process creation (4688). `AdjustTokenPrivileges` can only enable/disable privileges already present in a token; this event does not mean a new privilege was granted. Normal operating-system and management software dynamically adjusts token privileges, so every row requires process/account/service context. No process path or account is silently allowlisted in the base SPL, and no compliance or confirmed-ATT&CK claim is made.
evidence: After deployment, retain the approved Audit Token Right Adjusted policy and rollout scope; expected process/account/service privilege-enablement baseline with owner and version; Windows builds; canary 4703 XML and field aliases; effective Security-log XML input and `btool`; forwarder and `Splunk_TA_windows` versions; the `windows_high_risk_token_privilege_enabled` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and triggered-alert records; each result's UTC window, destination, process path/PID, subject and target account/SID/logon IDs, matched privilege set, record IDs, and source metadata; correlated 4688 process tree/command line, 4672/4673/4674, Sysmon/EDR process-access and image-signature/hash evidence, service/task/WMI activity, interactive/remote logon, software deployment, and asset/owner context; audit-policy/source-health and volume results; bounded notification exceptions; analyst disposition; and dated positive, negative, high-volume, duplicate, delayed-ingestion, and end-to-end controls. This documentation-only review enabled no audit policy, adjusted no token, executed no process, and created no Windows event, Splunk event, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest a redacted XML Event 4703 fixture with `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, `Provider_Name=Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing`, `Computer=win01.example.test`, `ProcessName=C:\\Lab\\token-test.exe`, `ProcessId=0x4d2`, `SubjectUserName=svc-lab`, `TargetUserName=svc-lab`, `EnabledPrivilegeList=SeChangeNotifyPrivilege SeImpersonatePrivilege SeDebugPrivilege`, and `EventRecordID=7001` in the closed window. Expect exactly one row whose `high_risk_privileges` contains both selected names and whose process/account/record identity matches the fixture.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated fixtures and expect zero rows for: Event 4703 with only `SeChangeNotifyPrivilege`; selected names present only in `DisabledPrivilegeList`; Event 4673 with `SeTcbPrivilege`; Event 4704 assigning `SeDebugPrivilege`; Event 4703 from another provider/source; a selected name embedded inside a longer token; malformed EventCode; missing destination or process path; and an otherwise positive event in the newest excluded five minutes. Ingest one normal `svchost.exe` Configuration Manager fixture that enables a selected privilege and confirm it remains a result until an evidence-backed post-detection exception is explicitly applied.

dataSources: Windows Security Event ID 4703 collected in XML through the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows. The SPL uses the deployment-local `index=wineventlog`, Microsoft-defined Security channel rendered as `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, and `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Required fields are `_time`, `Computer` or `host`, `EventCode` or `EventID`, `Provider_Name`, `ProcessName`, `ProcessId`, `EnabledPrivilegeList`, `DisabledPrivilegeList`, `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, `SubjectLogonId`, `TargetUserSid`, `TargetUserName`, `TargetDomainName`, `TargetLogonId`, `EventRecordID` or `RecordNumber`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. Event 4703 requires the Audit Token Right Adjusted/Audit Authorization Policy Change success audit, which Microsoft describes as high volume and disabled by default in relevant guidance; measure before broad deployment.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1 for XML Security-log collection and field extraction. A local security-content app should own the audit input override, field-validation checks, saved search, reviewed exception lookup, and dashboard. Splunk Enterprise Security is optional; no premium app is required.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4703 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), dest=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host))), provider=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName), process_path=lower(trim(ProcessName)), process_id=tostring(ProcessId), enabled_privileges=trim(EnabledPrivilegeList), subject=coalesce(SubjectUserSid,SubjectUserName,"not_extracted"), subject_user=coalesce(SubjectUserName,"not_extracted"), subject_domain=coalesce(SubjectDomainName,"not_extracted"), subject_logon_id=tostring(coalesce(SubjectLogonId,"not_extracted")), target_user=coalesce(TargetUserName,"not_extracted"), target_domain=coalesce(TargetDomainName,"not_extracted"), target_logon_id=tostring(coalesce(TargetLogonId,"not_extracted")), record_id=tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,"not_extracted"))
| where event_code=4703 AND provider="Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing" AND len(dest)>0 AND len(process_path)>0 AND match(enabled_privileges,"(?i)(^|\\s)Se(CreateToken|AssignPrimaryToken|Impersonate|Tcb|Debug|LoadDriver)Privilege(\\s|$)")
| rex max_match=0 field=enabled_privileges "(?i)(?<high_risk_privilege>Se(?:CreateToken|AssignPrimaryToken|Impersonate|Tcb|Debug|LoadDriver)Privilege)"
| eval high_risk_privileges=mvjoin(mvdedup(high_risk_privilege),","), use_case="UC-1.2.55"
| stats earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen count as events values(record_id) as record_ids values(high_risk_privileges) as high_risk_privileges by dest process_path process_id subject subject_user subject_domain subject_logon_id target_user target_domain target_logon_id source sourcetype use_case
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| table first_seen last_seen dest process_path process_id subject subject_user subject_domain subject_logon_id target_user target_domain target_logon_id high_risk_privileges events record_ids source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 -last_seen dest process_path
description: Reports one row per destination, process, and subject/target token context when Security Event 4703 shows that the process enabled at least one of six explicitly selected high-risk token privileges in the closed five-minute window. The result preserves the matched privilege names and Windows record IDs without claiming the subsequent privileged action occurred.
value: Enabling token-creation, primary-token assignment, impersonation, trusted-computing-base, debug, or driver-load privileges creates a high-value investigation point before or alongside privilege escalation, credential access, code injection, or kernel activity. Process/account baselining and correlation shorten triage by distinguishing expected operating-system behavior from an unusual binary or service context while preserving the exact token change for response.
implementation: Pilot Audit Token Right Adjusted success auditing on representative hosts, measure Event 4703 volume, and validate XML fields before rollout. Collect Security XML with `Splunk_TA_windows`; save the SPL as `windows_high_risk_token_privilege_enabled`; run every 5 minutes over the delayed closed window; and create one case per `dest,process_path,subject_logon_id,target_logon_id`, preserving all privileges and record IDs. Do not embed broad Windows-process exclusions. Validate each selected privilege, disabled-only and substring negatives, normal Configuration Manager/WMI volume, duplicate collection, process correlation, source silence, alert delivery, and bounded post-detection exceptions.
visualization: Build a token-privilege dashboard with audit-policy/source freshness and Event 4703 volume first; single values for affected hosts, processes, and target logon sessions; a timechart by high-risk privilege; a table with process, subject/target accounts, logon IDs, privilege set, count, and case state; and a process-by-privilege heat map. Drill down to the raw 4703, process creation/tree, file hash/signature/path, 4672/4673/4674, EDR/Sysmon process access, service/task/WMI execution, software deployment, and logon/session evidence. Label the signal “privilege enabled,” not “token theft confirmed.”
schema: Native Windows Security Event 4703 token-right adjustment XML
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM data model is claimed. CIM Change and Endpoint.Processes do not preserve the Event 4703 enabled/disabled privilege lists, subject/target token context, logon IDs, provider, and event record ID. If scale requires a summary, preserve one event-grain row per destination/source/record ID with process path/PID, subject/target SIDs and logon IDs, enabled/disabled lists, matched privileges, event time, and ingestion/duplicate markers.

knownFalsePositives:
A matched row is a real enablement of at least one selected privilege in the reported token context. Legitimate software can do this dynamically, so benign cause—not event falsity—is the main tuning problem.

1. **Microsoft Configuration Manager or WMI activity through `svchost.exe`** — Microsoft explicitly documents recurring WMI queries as a high-volume 4703 source. Distinguish by service hosting context, expected Configuration Manager client/version, WMI operation, stable binary signature/hash, service SID/account, deployment schedule, and established privilege set. Use a tuple-bound exception; never allowlist all `svchost.exe`.

2. **Endpoint security, EDR, antimalware, or forensic tooling** — Security products may enable SeDebugPrivilege or driver-related privilege for protected-process inspection. Verify product, signer, hash, installed version, service identity, policy/job, management-console evidence, process tree, target process, and owner. Signed status alone is insufficient.

3. **Backup, restore, imaging, or disaster-recovery software** — Agents can adjust powerful token privileges while taking snapshots or restoring systems. Correlate job ID, protected asset, approved schedule, vendor binary/hash/signature, service account, exact privileges, and storage activity. Do not suppress outside the job's exclusive UTC bounds.

4. **Driver, firmware, or hardware-management deployment** — Vendor management services can enable SeLoadDriverPrivilege during approved installation. Verify package/change ID, catalog signature, hash, target device/driver, deployment ring, installer process tree, and later driver/code-integrity state.

5. **SQL Server, IIS, virtualization, clustering, or other privileged Windows services** — Service accounts and hosts can legitimately adjust impersonation or primary-token privileges. Baseline the exact service name, binary path/hash, account SID, logon type/session, privilege set, host role, and workload operation; product name or path alone is not an exception.

6. **Administrative debugging or incident-response session** — Authorized debuggers and response tools may enable SeDebugPrivilege. Match incident/change ID, named operator, privileged-access session, approved tool hash, destination, start/end, and target. Preserve the row as case evidence.

7. **Authorized atomic/control test** — A lab utility may intentionally call AdjustTokenPrivileges. Require test ID, signed/hash-pinned binary, isolated host, operator, exact privilege, UTC bounds, alert and cleanup proof. Suppress only duplicate notification after test identity is established.

8. **Duplicate Security-log collection** — Local plus WEF inputs can index one record twice. Compare destination, provider, channel, EventRecordID, event time, and raw hash. Fix collection; do not collapse distinct record IDs or repeated adjustments.

**Safe suppression:** preserve raw 4703 and the base result. Apply notification exceptions after detection through a reviewed lookup keyed to exact destination/role, full process path plus approved hash/signer/version, account SID, matched privilege set, operational job/change/test ID, owner, approver, and exclusive epoch bounds. Reject basename-only, directory-wide, signer-wide, account-wide, permanent, wildcard, or all-Windows-process exclusions; never suppress source/audit-policy loss, unknown binaries, path/hash drift, privilege-set expansion, repeated unexplained sessions, or missing corroboration.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Microsoft Security Event 4703, Audit Token Right Adjusted, advanced audit policy, AdjustTokenPrivileges, and privilege definitions; MITRE ATT&CK T1134 and Splunk Security Content were used as investigative context without claiming Event 4703 proves token manipulation; audit enablement, volume, XML extraction, fixtures, token adjustment, process correlation, exceptions, SPL, alert delivery, and production response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Windows security/Splunk/endpoint-security SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: The scheduled SPL is narrow and scans one EventCode over 5 minutes, but Microsoft rates Token Right Adjustment auditing high volume and warns that dynamic applications/services can generate many 4703 events. Pilot events/second, bytes, Security-log retention/overwrite, lag, and cost by host role before rollout.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and semantic boundary

Assign Windows security/audit-policy, endpoint detection, identity/PAM, application/service, Splunk collection/content, telemetry-health, and incident owners. Inventory host role, criticality, Windows build, installed management/security/backup/application services, expected service accounts and SIDs, stable process paths/hashes/signers/versions, privileges each process legitimately enables, job/change context, maintenance authority, and retirement state. Treat this as a behavior baseline, not a static list of “safe executable names.”

Replace the original 4673/4674 “token manipulation” claim. Those events record privileged service/object operations, not token changes. Microsoft defines Event 4703 as token privileges enabled or disabled for an account token and exposes process, subject, target, enabled list, and disabled list. `AdjustTokenPrivileges` cannot add a privilege absent from the token; it changes the enabled state of existing privileges. The selected names are high-impact investigation signals, but the event alone does not prove which API called it, what object/action followed, or malicious token manipulation.

Microsoft documents Event 4703 under Audit Token Right Adjusted/Audit Authorization Policy Change, with high volume and no failure events for the token-right-adjusted subcategory. Dynamic applications and services, including Configuration Manager WMI activity through `svchost.exe`, can generate many events. Pilot on each role and ensure Security-log retention and forwarding remain safe before fleet rollout. Do not enable broad auditing merely to satisfy this document.

## Step 1 — Enable, collect, and verify Event 4703

Apply Advanced Audit Policy through a controlled GPO ring and verify effective policy with the approved Windows audit-policy method. Enable success auditing only where risk, storage, and operational ownership justify it. Avoid mixing legacy and advanced audit policy without the organization's supported precedence design. Monitor policy drift and Security-log overwrite separately.

Install `Splunk_TA_windows` from Splunkbase 742. Collect the Security channel in XML through a local `inputs.conf` stanza owned by the deployment app; `index=wineventlog` is the local choice and `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`/`source=XmlWinEventLog:Security` must match observed metadata. Inspect `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, avoid duplicate local/WEF routes, and restrict Security-log data. The Splunk service account/forwarder needs only documented read/forward permissions.

Capture canary XML for 4703 and verify all required fields. Keep `ProcessId` and logon IDs in their original hexadecimal/string form to correlate exactly with 4688/4624; convert only in a separate validated field if needed. Confirm `EnabledPrivilegeList` and `DisabledPrivilegeList` tokenization uses whitespace and `-` for absent values where observed. Validate provider `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing`, record ID, original computer identity under WEF, and event version. Never infer an enabled privilege from the disabled list or message text.

Build source-health/data-quality searches for expected host with no Security telemetry in 15 minutes, no 4703 after a scheduled safe canary where expected, audit-policy drift, Event 1102/104 log clear, channel near overwrite, missing process/privilege/account fields, unknown event version, future time, lag over 10 minutes, and duplicate destination/source/record ID. Alert telemetry owners separately.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the search

Save the SPL as `windows_high_risk_token_privilege_enabled`; schedule every 5 minutes. At 12:15, `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` searches 12:05–12:10 and leaves 5 minutes for ingestion. Measure p95/p99 delay and move both bounds together. Trigger on each result; group case updates by `dest,process_path,subject_logon_id,target_logon_id` for 30 minutes while preserving every distinct record ID and expanded privilege set.

The base clause selects the exact local index/source/source type/EventCode. Normalization keeps destination, provider, process, account/session identity, lists, and record ID. The `where` clause enforces exact provider, nonempty identity/process, and token-boundary matching for six names. This avoids substring collisions. `rex max_match=0` extracts every selected enabled privilege; `mvdedup` and `mvjoin` make the set visible. `stats` aggregates only the same process and subject/target context inside one closed window.

`SeCreateTokenPrivilege` permits token creation; `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` supports replacing a process-level token; `SeImpersonatePrivilege` supports impersonating an authenticated client; `SeTcbPrivilege` identifies trusted-computing-base capability; `SeDebugPrivilege` permits powerful process inspection; and `SeLoadDriverPrivilege` supports device-driver load/unload. Their inclusion is a risk policy, not proof of a specific ATT&CK sub-technique. Do not label every result T1134. Correlate subsequent process/token/handle activity.

No process is excluded in the base SPL. Apply reviewed exception enrichment after detection, so drift remains measurable. Do not use the old `NOT match(ProcessName,"lsass|svchost|...")`: attackers can inject, replace, or mimic trusted processes, and legitimate instances need full path/hash/service context.

## Step 3 — Validate fields, volume, detections, and negatives

Use isolated fixtures first. Assert that one event containing two selected names returns one row and both names; test each six names separately. Test list order, multiple whitespace, case behavior, `-`, null, neighboring privilege names, selected names only in `DisabledPrivilegeList`, embedded substrings, wrong provider/source/EventCode, missing destination/process, duplicate record, delayed arrival, and earliest/latest boundaries. Ensure all negative controls return zero.

Measure Event 4703 rate and bytes for at least 7 days per representative domain controller, member server, workstation, Configuration Manager client, EDR agent, backup server, SQL/IIS host, and virtualization/cluster role. Identify top process path/hash/account/privilege tuples and verify each with owners. Check Security-log overwrite, forwarder queues, index lag, scheduler skips, and search runtime. Do not suppress a tuple merely because it is frequent.

For an end-to-end lab test, use a reviewed hash-pinned utility or vendor-supported action that enables a privilege already present in its token. Never grant a new user right or run exploit tooling on production for test convenience. Capture process creation/hash/signature, Event 4703, alert delivery, and cleanup. Test disabled-only behavior through a safe supported action if available. Test Configuration Manager/WMI known volume and confirm an exception would match only the exact approved tuple/time/context.

Record Windows/audit-policy/forwarder/TA/Splunk versions, fixture hashes, test utility hash, exact UTC bounds, expected/actual rows, search SID, alert/case, and source health. Keep `status=draft` until Windows security, endpoint, identity, application, Splunk, and response owners accept volume, baseline, controls, exceptions, and runbook.

## Step 4 — Triage and response

For each row: (1) verify raw 4703 provider/channel/record and enabled list; (2) identify full process path, PID, hash, signature, version, parent/child tree, and service/task/WMI host context; (3) resolve subject and target SIDs/accounts/logon IDs to 4624/4672 session and PAM ticket; (4) compare the exact privilege set with approved baseline; (5) inspect 4688 command line and Sysmon/EDR process access, handle duplication, injection, child creation, driver load, credential access, and network behavior; (6) check software deployment/backup/security/administrative job; and (7) determine whether the privilege was disabled later or the process ended.

Escalate unknown/untrusted binaries, user-writable paths, signer/hash/version drift, unusual parent, interactive user context, new target account/session, privilege-set expansion, enabling on high-value servers, correlation with LSASS/winlogon access, SYSTEM child creation, unsigned/unapproved driver activity, suspicious network/logon behavior, or missing owner/job. Repeated high-volume events may indicate compromise or misconfiguration and also threaten audit availability.

Do not automatically terminate the process, disable an account, strip token privileges, change user-right assignment, stop a security/backup service, unload a driver, or reboot from this signal. Token and service changes can destabilize Windows and destroy evidence. Follow endpoint-response and service-owner runbooks. Containment urgency depends on corroboration and asset risk.

## Step 5 — Troubleshooting

- **No 4703:** verify effective Token Right Adjusted/Audit Authorization Policy Change success policy, Windows build, actual Security log, event volume, input, source type/source, index, role permissions, and lag. Some builds/policies/stacks may not emit expected test behavior; document coverage.
- **Huge volume:** identify exact process/hash/service/account/privilege tuples, especially Configuration Manager/WMI. Increase capacity or narrowly tune after detection; do not disable evidence without risk acceptance.
- **Enabled list is null:** inspect raw XML, TA version, event version, and parsing. Never substitute disabled privileges or message text without a versioned test.
- **Process ID does not join 4688:** preserve hexadecimal format, destination, boot/session time, and event timing. PID reuse requires narrow temporal correlation; absence of 4688 may indicate process-audit/source gaps.
- **Trusted filename in unusual path:** treat path/hash/signature/parent drift as suspicious. Basename allowlists are forbidden.
- **`svchost.exe` noise:** resolve hosted service/WMI activity and Configuration Manager evidence. Do not globally suppress `svchost.exe`.
- **Distinct privileges collapse:** inspect `rex max_match=0`, multivalue extraction, whitespace, and `mvdedup`; keep full raw enabled list in drilldown.
- **Duplicate rows:** compare destination/source/record ID and local/WEF routes. Fix collection; preserve distinct adjustments.
- **ATT&CK mapping disputed:** the event is privilege-state adjustment evidence only. Remove tactic labels from case routing unless corroborating behavior supports them.
- **Source goes silent after enabling audit:** investigate log overwrite, forwarder pressure, policy rollback, or tampering; silence is not healthy.
grandmaExplanation: Windows programs can switch on powerful abilities they already have, such as acting for another user or inspecting other programs. We flag those moments so the team can check whether the program and account were expected.
hardware: Windows 10/11 and supported Windows Server systems capable of Event 4703 under Audit Token Right Adjusted/Audit Authorization Policy Change. Audit behavior and volume must be canary-tested by build and installed management stack.
